ukmt-smc-2024-01.title: Work with the decimal
ukmt-smc-2024-01.body:
$0.252525\ldots\times 0.4$: $0.25\times0.4=0.10$ and the pattern repeats every two places, giving $0.101010\ldots=0.\dot1\dot0$.

**Answer: (E)**

ukmt-smc-2024-02.title: Estimate by orders of magnitude
ukmt-smc-2024-02.body:
$4800\approx5\times10^3$ and $0.000018\approx2\times10^{-5}$, so the quotient is about $2.5\times10^8$; the only option of that size is 270 000 000.

**Answer: (A)**

ukmt-smc-2024-03.title: Opposite faces sum to 7
ukmt-smc-2024-03.body:
On a standard die opposite faces sum to 7. On each die, the four side faces form two opposite pairs, so they total $2\times7=14$ per die, i.e. $28$ for both dice. The remaining visible face is the top of the upper die, $n=33-28=5$. The bottom face of the upper die is opposite, so it is $7-5=2$, and this is the touching number.

**Answer: (B) 2**

ukmt-smc-2024-03.title: Total of all faces
ukmt-smc-2024-03.body:
Each die has total $1+\dots+6=21$. The hidden faces are: the bottom of the lower die (touching table), and the touching face of each die. Let the touching number be $t$; the touching face of the lower die is $t$ (top of lower die) and of the upper die is $t$ (bottom). The bottom of the lower die is $7-t$. Hidden total $=t+t+(7-t)=7+t$. So $42-(7+t)=33$, giving $t=2$.

**Answer: (B) 2**

ukmt-smc-2024-04.title: Angle sum
ukmt-smc-2024-04.body:
$x+7x+x^2=180\Rightarrow x^2+8x-180=0\Rightarrow(x+18)(x-10)=0$. Since $x>0$, $x=10$, so the angles are $10^\circ,70^\circ,100^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $100^{\circ}$**

ukmt-smc-2024-04.title: Guess and check
ukmt-smc-2024-04.body:
The largest angle is $x^2$ when $x\ge 7$, so it is one of the options and $x$ is its square root. Try $x^2=100$: $x=10$ and $10+70+100=180$, which works.

**Answer: (C) $100^{\circ}$**

ukmt-smc-2024-06.title: Count edges at the octagon
ukmt-smc-2024-06.body:
The octagon has 8 vertices and 8 edges. At least three edges meet at every vertex, so each octagon vertex has an edge that is not an edge of the octagon. That edge cannot join two octagon vertices (they all lie in the plane of the face), so it goes to a vertex off the face. These 8 extra edges are all different because each has exactly one end on the octagon. So there are at least $8+8=16$ edges. An octagonal pyramid has exactly 16 edges.

**Answer: (D) 16**

ukmt-smc-2024-06.title: Check with Euler's formula
ukmt-smc-2024-06.body:
The octagonal pyramid has $V=9$, $E=16$, $F=9$, and $V-E+F=2$, so it is a valid solid. The counting argument shows fewer than 16 edges is impossible.

**Answer: (D) 16**

ukmt-smc-2024-08.title: Sum of remaining four
ukmt-smc-2024-08.body:
The remaining four sum to $4\times11x=44x$. All five sum to $60x$. The removed expression is $60x-44x=16x$.

**Answer: (D) $16x$**

ukmt-smc-2024-08.title: Mean of all five
ukmt-smc-2024-08.body:
The mean of all five is $12x$. Removing a term below the mean raises the mean; removing one above lowers it. The new mean $11x$ is $x$ lower, and removing $t$ changes the mean to $\frac{60x-t}{4}=11x$, so $t=16x$.

**Answer: (D)**

ukmt-smc-2024-09.title: Divisibility by 2 and 9
ukmt-smc-2024-09.body:
To be even, the last digit (equal to the first) must be even; the largest choice is 8. Write the number as $8bc\,cb8$. Its digit sum is $2(8+b+c)$, which must be a multiple of 9, so $8+b+c$ is a multiple of 9. Since $8+b+c\le26$, we need $8+b+c=9$ or $18$. To maximise the number take $8+b+c=18$, so $b+c=10$, with $b$ as large as possible: $b=9$, $c=1$. The number is $891198$, whose hundreds digit is 1.

**Answer: (E) 1**

ukmt-smc-2024-09.title: Check
ukmt-smc-2024-09.body:
$891198=18\times49511$. A larger palindrome would start with 9 (odd, not allowed) or with 8 and $b=9$, $c\ge2$, whose digit sum $2(17+c)$ is not a multiple of 9 for $c=2,\dots,9$.

**Answer: (E) 1**

ukmt-smc-2024-10.title: List by prime content
ukmt-smc-2024-10.body:
Two-digit factors: multiples of 11 only: $11,22,44,88$; involving 23 (not 11): $23,46,92$; involving both 11 and 23: $253>99$, none. Total $4+3=7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

ukmt-smc-2024-11.title: Test and prove
ukmt-smc-2024-11.body:
$n=1$: A gives 2, B gives 3, C gives 7, none square. $n=2$: E gives $2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6+1=721$, not square (it lies between $26^2=676$ and $27^2=729$). For D: $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)+1=(n^2+3n)(n^2+3n+2)+1=(n^2+3n+1)^2$, a square for every $n$.

**Answer: (D)**

ukmt-smc-2024-11.title: Substitution
ukmt-smc-2024-11.body:
Let $m=n^2+3n+1$. Then $n(n+3)=m-1$ and $(n+1)(n+2)=m+1$, so the product plus 1 is $(m-1)(m+1)+1=m^2$.

**Answer: (D)**

ukmt-smc-2024-12.title: Units and tens digits
ukmt-smc-2024-12.body:
Eight digits $1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9$ are used. A two-digit prime ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9 (not even, not 5), so the four units digits are $1,3,7,9$ and the tens digits are $2,4,6,8$. Hence $p+q+r+s=10(2+4+6+8)+(1+3+7+9)=200+20=220$. (Such primes exist, e.g. $23,41,67,89$.)

**Answer: (A) 220**

ukmt-smc-2024-12.title: Example
ukmt-smc-2024-12.body:
$23+41+67+89=220$, and the argument above shows the sum does not depend on the pairing.

**Answer: (A) 220**

ukmt-smc-2024-13.title: Label the bottom row
ukmt-smc-2024-13.body:
Bottom row $1,a,b,10$. Second row: $1+a,\ a+b,\ b+10$. Third row: $1+2a+b,\ a+2b+10$. Top: $3a+3b+11=2024$, so $a+b=671$. The brick $z$ is the middle of the second row, $a+b=671$.

**Answer: (C) 671**

ukmt-smc-2024-13.title: Weights
ukmt-smc-2024-13.body:
The top number is $1\cdot1+3a+3b+1\cdot10$ (binomial weights $1,3,3,1$). So $3(a+b)=2024-11=2013$ and $a+b=671=z$.

**Answer: (C) 671**

ukmt-smc-2024-14.title: Use the last digits
ukmt-smc-2024-14.body:
A prime greater than 5 ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9, so $S$ and $T$ are 1 and 3 in some order, and $P,Q,R$ are 2, 4, 5. Try each value of $R$. If $R=4$ then $\{P,Q\}=\{2,5\}$ and the numbers are $\{241,543\}$ or $\{243,541\}$; $543$ and $243$ are multiples of 3. If $R=5$ then $\{P,Q\}=\{2,4\}$ and the numbers are $\{251,453\}$ or $\{253,451\}$; $453=3\times151$, $253=11\times23$. If $R=2$ then $\{P,Q\}=\{4,5\}$: $421$ and $523$ are both prime. So $R=2$.

**Answer: (B) 2**

ukmt-smc-2024-15.title: Two equations
ukmt-smc-2024-15.body:
Let $KL=x$ and $KN=y$. The shaded region is the larger square minus the smaller square, so $x^2-y^2=62$. Triangle $NKL$ is right-angled at $K$, so $x^2+y^2=10^2=100$. Subtracting, $2y^2=38$, so $y=\sqrt{19}$.

**Answer: (C) $\sqrt{19}$**

ukmt-smc-2024-16.title: Cases by number of red corners
ukmt-smc-2024-16.body:
Label the top row $A,B,C,D$ and the bottom row $E,F,G,H$; the corners are $A,D,E,H$. All three red doors are corners: 4 ways (choose which corner stays blue; both rows are then covered). Exactly two corners red, in different rows ($AE,AH,DE,DH$): the third red door is one of the 4 middle doors, 4 ways each, 16 ways. Exactly two corners red, in the same row: for $AD$ the third door must be in the bottom row and not a corner, $F$ or $G$; similarly for $EH$ the third is $B$ or $C$: 4 ways. Total $4+16+4=24$.

**Answer: (B) 24**

ukmt-smc-2024-16.title: Complementary counting
ukmt-smc-2024-16.body:
Triples with at least one red door in each row: $\binom83-2\binom43=56-8=48$. Remove those with 0 corners red: the three red doors are 3 of the 4 middle doors ($B,C,F,G$), always covering both rows: 4. Remove those with exactly 1 corner red: choose the corner (4 ways), then two middle doors, 6 pairs, but not both in the corner's own row (otherwise the other row is empty): 5 pairs; $4\times5=20$. So $48-4-20=24$.

**Answer: (B) 24**

ukmt-smc-2024-17.title: Find the number of red balls
ukmt-smc-2024-17.body:
Let there be $n$ red balls. $P(\text{both red})=\frac n4\cdot\frac{n-1}3=\frac12$, so $n^2-n-6=0$, $(n-3)(n+2)=0$, so $n=3$. One white ball means two white balls cannot be drawn: probability $0$.

**Answer: (E) 0**

ukmt-smc-2024-17.title: Try each number of reds
ukmt-smc-2024-17.body:
$P(\text{both red})$ is $0,0,\frac1{6},\frac12,1$ for $n=0,1,2,3,4$ reds (e.g. $n=3$: $\frac34\cdot\frac23=\frac12$). So $n=3$, leaving one white ball.

**Answer: (E) 0**

ukmt-smc-2024-18.title: Compare areas
ukmt-smc-2024-18.body:
The inner circle is cut into 4 equal pieces, so each piece has area $\frac\pi4$. There are 14 pieces of equal area, so the whole disc has area $14\cdot\frac\pi4=\frac{7\pi}2$. The outer radius $1+x$ satisfies $\pi(1+x)^2=\frac{7\pi}2$, so $1+x=\sqrt{\frac72}=\frac{\sqrt{14}}2$ and $x=\frac{\sqrt{14}}2-1$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{\sqrt{14}}2-1$**

ukmt-smc-2024-18.title: Ratio of areas
ukmt-smc-2024-18.body:
Total area : inner area $=14:4=7:2$. Areas scale as the square of the radius, so $(1+x)^2:1=7:2$, giving $1+x=\sqrt{7/2}=\frac{\sqrt{14}}2$.

**Answer: (C)**

ukmt-smc-2024-19.title: Deduce the hands
ukmt-smc-2024-19.body:
Paolo scores 4 with cards $1,3$ (the cards are different, so $2+2$ is not possible). All twelve cards sum to 78 and the five scores sum to 70, so the two unused cards sum to 8; with 1 and 3 used they are $2$ and $6$. Thomas (20) has $12,8$ or $11,9$. If Thomas has $11,9$, then Stephen (19) has $12,7$ (the other pairs $11,8$ and $10,9$ use a card Thomas holds), and Romy (16) cannot be formed from the remaining cards $4,5,8,10$. So Thomas has $12,8$; then Stephen has $10,9$, Romy has $11,5$ and Quinn has $7,4$. Only statement C is true.

**Answer: (C) Romy has card 5**

ukmt-smc-2024-20.title: Rearrange
ukmt-smc-2024-20.body:
$y=\frac{20x}{x-20}=20+\frac{400}{x-20}$. For $y>0$ we need $x>20$, and $y$ is largest when $x-20$ is as small as possible: $x=21$, $y=20+400=420$.

**Answer: (D) 420**

ukmt-smc-2024-20.title: Factorise
ukmt-smc-2024-20.body:
$\frac1x+\frac1y=\frac1{20}$ gives $(x-20)(y-20)=400$. The largest $y$ comes from $x-20=1$, $y-20=400$, so $y=420$.

**Answer: (D) 420**

ukmt-smc-2024-21.title: Start with 2 Down
ukmt-smc-2024-21.body:
2 Down is a three-digit multiple of $13\times19=247$ with distinct digits: $247$ or $741$ ($494$ and $988$ repeat digits). Its last digit is the last digit of 3 Across, a square, and squares do not end in 7, so 2 Down $=741$. 3 Across is a three-digit square ending in 1 with no 4 or 7: $361$ or $961$. 1 Down is a multiple of 11 starting at the top-left, ending in 3 or 9 (the first digit of 3 Across): possibilities from the remaining digits are $253$, $583$ (ending 3) or $539$ (ending 9). 1 Across is a multiple of 9 so its digits sum to a multiple of 9; with $1\,\text{Down}=583$ or $539$ the middle digit would have to be 6, which is already used. So 1 Down $=253$, 1 Across $=297$, 3 Across $=361$ (2 Down $=741$). The digits used are $2,5,3,9,7,4,6,1$, so 8 is missing.

**Answer: (B) 8**

ukmt-smc-2024-21.title: Check the completed grid
ukmt-smc-2024-21.body:
Grid: row 1: $2\,9\,7$; row 2: $5\,\blacksquare\,4$; row 3: $3\,6\,1$. $297=9\times33$, $361=19^2$, $253=11\times23$, $741=3\times13\times19=3\times247$. All digits $1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9$ are used exactly once, so 8 is not used.

**Answer: (B) 8**

ukmt-smc-2024-22.title: Compare bases and heights
ukmt-smc-2024-22.body:
The four small triangles have total area $4+8+12+8=32=[FGH]$, and the three on the $FG$ side form $[FGI]=4+8+12=24$. Triangles $FGI$ and $FGH$ have the same height from $G$ to line $FH$, so $IH:FH=(32-24):32=1:4$. Triangle $FKI$ has area $4+8=12$, half of $[FGI]=24$; they share the base $FI$, so $K$ is at half the distance of $G$ from line $FI$. (Equivalently $K$ is the midpoint of $FG$.) Then $[IKH]=\frac12\cdot IH\cdot d(K,FH)=\frac12\cdot\frac14FH\cdot\frac12d(G,FH)=\frac18[FGH]=4$.

**Answer: (A) 4**

ukmt-smc-2024-22.title: Using the midpoint
ukmt-smc-2024-22.body:
$[FKI]=12=\frac12[FGI]$ gives $FK=\frac12FG$, so $K$ is the midpoint of $FG$ and $[FKH]=\frac12[FGH]=16$. Triangles $FKH$ and $IKH$ share the vertex $K$ and have bases $FH$ and $IH=\frac14FH$ on the same line, so $[IKH]=\frac14\cdot16=4$.

**Answer: (A) 4**

ukmt-smc-2024-23.title: Find the kite
ukmt-smc-2024-23.body:
Each kite has a line of symmetry, so the two angles meeting the axis are equal. Where three kites meet the angle is $120^\circ$, where four meet it is $90^\circ$ (two such angles), so the kite has angles $120^\circ,90^\circ,90^\circ,60^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$). Half of a kite is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle with legs $x$ and $y=\sqrt3x$. The kite has area $2\cdot\frac{xy}2=\sqrt3x^2$ and it equals $\frac{8\sqrt3}8=\sqrt3$, so $x=1$, $y=\sqrt3$. The boundary of the hat consists of 8 short sides of length $x=1$ and 6 long sides of length $y=\sqrt3$: perimeter $8+6\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (E) $8+6\sqrt3$**

ukmt-smc-2024-24.title: Cycle of three values
ukmt-smc-2024-24.body:
Put $x=3$: $f(3)+f(-\tfrac12)=72$. Put $x=-\frac12$: $f(-\tfrac12)+f(\tfrac23)=-12$. Put $x=\frac23$: $f(\tfrac23)+f(3)=16$. Adding the first and third and subtracting the second: $2f(3)=72+16-(-12)=100$, so $f(3)=50$.

**Answer: (E) 50**

ukmt-smc-2024-25.title: Equal areas
ukmt-smc-2024-25.body:
The three semicircles are congruent. Let the regions be as in the official solution: $P$ is the part of the semicircle centred at $X$ in the $30^\circ$ sector, so its area is $\frac{30}{180}\cdot24=4$. The lens-type regions $P+Q$ and $Q+R$ are congruent, so $R=P=4$. The region $P+Q$ (two overlapping $60^\circ$ sectors minus an equilateral triangle) has the same area as $Q+S$ (a $120^\circ$ sector minus two $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles whose total area is that of the equilateral triangle), so $S=P=4$. Total shaded area $=4+4+4=12$.

**Answer: (A) 12**
